Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

issues.item: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other selected items describe fear-based reactivity, hypervigilance, sexual trauma triggers, and intrusive/reliving memory phenomena after rape. In that context, prominent risk-taking pulls in the opposite direction of the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation and is not supported by appraisals or maladaptive-strategy items. This creates a within-node and cross-node coherence problem.

vignette: Meera had been checking irrigation lines along the northern boundary of a rented California vineyard when a man stepped from the tree line. He had pinned her against a rusted fence post while a stray dog barked relentlessly nearby, its voice echoing across the dry rows. He had forced himself on her, his weight crushing the air from her lungs, until he finally released her and disappeared into the heat. Over the next several months, the vineyard began to feel like a live wire. Now, at sixty-one, Meera still worked the land, walking the furrows for the family estate, but the daily routine had become a series of sudden alarms. Whenever a dog approached the vineyard gates-even a neighbor's gentle retriever-her chest would lock before she could even identify the animal. Her body would brace for impact, muscles tightening, breath shortening, as if the old attacker were emerging from the rows again. She had come to believe her nervous system had turned traitor, bracing for violence the moment a canine crossed her path. Concurrently, memories of the assault would slide into her awareness without warning, playing back like a reel of film she could not stop. She saw the weathered post, felt the suffocating pressure on her ribs, and for a breath, she was back in the dirt with him. The film of the frightening event repeated itself, unspooling in her mind during quiet moments in the packing shed or while washing the dust from her hands. When she remembered the frightening event, she felt like it was happening right now, her shoulders hunched and her gaze fixed on the ground. She had learned to keep her eyes down, avoiding the sight of any animal that might cross her path, and she had stopped bringing her lunch into the field to avoid lingering near the tree line. This state of hypervigilance reshaped her nights and her marriage. When her husband, Arjun, would place a hand on her shoulder from behind while she harvested grapes or poured evening tea, Meera would jump back as if struck, reacting with alarm when someone touched her unexpectedly. She told him she needed to stay alert, that the house never felt safe enough to drop her guard, and he had learned to sleep on the far edge of the bed. She avoided intimacy altogether, convincing herself that any sexual situation would inevitably lead back to that field, to the loss of control she could not tolerate. At work, she began taking the long route past the property office to avoid the farm manager's border collie, and she started calling in sick when her shoulders ached from tension, trading steady paychecks for a fragile sense of safety. She would lie perfectly still under the sheets, listening to the house settle and the wind move through the trellises, afraid to drop her guard. The silence only made her muscles tense further. The pattern tightened with every passing season. A barking dog meant her body would fire before her mind could catch up, her muscles locking and breath shortening before she could even name the source of the fear. She had spent years walking the vineyard rows with her back to the trees, scanning for movement, exhausted by a vigilance that never switched off. When the terrier slipped through the broken fence, her chest tightened instantly, her body bracing for impact before she could process the animal's harmless posture. It was the morning she dropped a basket of grapes, her hands trembling from that automatic surge of dread, that she finally picked up the phone. She was tired of living as though the attack were still unfolding, and she wanted to know if her nerves could ever stop sounding the alarm.
